variants: in conformity with, in compliance with, and the one-word pursuant to are the near-synonyms of the same register; under and as required by are the plain-English replacements. In accordance to is an error, and so is in accordance of.
entries.meaning: States that an act conformed to a governing rule, standard, or instrument. It is compliance language, and in ordinary prose under, following, or as required by is nearly always the better choice.
examples: The audit was conducted in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards.
Ballots will be counted in accordance with state law.
The device must be installed in accordance with the manufacturer's specifications.
In accordance with your instructions, we canceled the order on Friday.
Benefits are calculated in accordance with the schedule in Appendix B.

entries.ipa: /ɪn dɪˈfɛns əv/ · weak /ɪn dɪˈfɛns ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund (in defense of doing nothing) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [clause] in defense of [noun phrase] / In defense of [noun phrase], [clause] / in [possessive] defense — the short alternative frame
entries.contrast: Against in support of, which backs a proposal, in defense of answers an attack — there has to be a criticism, a charge, or a threat somewhere in the picture. Against on behalf of, it implies no authorization: you may defend someone who never asked you to. In athletics, in defense of the title means the holder is trying to keep it.
variants: in defence of is the British spelling; American English uses defense. The possessive frame in her defense is idiomatic and far commoner than in defense of her. Note the stress: the sports noun meaning "the defending side" is /ˈdifɛns/, DEE-fenss, but inside this phrase the stress stays on the second syllable.
entries.meaning: Names what is being protected or argued for. Something has to be under threat for the phrase to make sense — a reputation, a flock, a championship — and that requirement is what separates it from the other support prepositions. 1. Arguing or acting to protect something under attack. 2. Physically protecting. 3. Defending a title or championship.
examples: He wrote a long letter in defense of the department's record.
She spoke in defense of a colleague nobody else would defend.
In defense of the old system, it never once lost a file.
The dog was shot in defense of the flock.
Two firefighters were injured in defense of the outbuildings.
She returns to Melbourne in January in defense of her title.
The team travels to Denver in defense of a nine-game winning streak.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈfeɪvər əv/ · weak /ɪn ˈfeɪvər ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund (in favor of raising the cap) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: be in favor of [noun phrase / verb-ing] / vote in favor of [noun phrase] / [drop/abandon X] in favor of [Y] / rule/decide/find in favor of [party]
entries.contrast: Three senses a reader has to keep apart. Sense 1 is approval, the opposite of against. Sense 2 is preference, and here the thing after the phrase is the option that won — the exact reverse of as opposed to, where what follows is the option rejected. Sense 3 is legal and financial and means "to the benefit of." Against plain for, sense 1 is the deliberative register: I'm for it in the hallway, I am in favor of the amendment on the record. Its listing among the complex prepositions generally is at in favor of.
variants: in favour of is British; American English drops the u. In X's favor is the possessive alternative: the ruling went in her favor.
entries.meaning: Declares approval of something, names the option that won a choice, or assigns a benefit. All three senses turn on the same idea of favor, but they attach to very different kinds of sentence and are easy to run together. 1. Supporting; approving of. 2. Chosen in place of — the surviving option follows the phrase. 3. To the legal or financial benefit of.
examples: Nine members voted in favor of the measure.
Are you in favor of moving the meeting to Thursday?
Public opinion has shifted sharply in favor of the plan.
The city dropped the streetcar plan in favor of dedicated bus lanes.
She turned down the corporate offer in favor of a research fellowship.
The court ruled in favor of the tenants.
Make the check payable in favor of the trust, not the individual.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈkipɪŋ wɪθ/ · weak /wəθ/ · also /wɪð/ before a vowel
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative headed by what (in keeping with what neighboring districts have offered) — never a finite clause; a gerund is grammatical but awkward
entries.pattern: [clause], in keeping with [noun phrase] / In keeping with [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Where in accordance with means conformity to a rule that binds, in keeping with means consistency with a spirit, a tradition, or a character — nobody is obliged. In accordance with the statute is legally required; in keeping with the family's wishes is fitting but optional. In line with sits between the two, and consistent with is the analytic version of the same idea. Its listing among the complex prepositions generally is at in keeping with.
entries.meaning: Says the act fits the tone or the precedent of whatever came before it. It is evaluative rather than regulatory, which is why it collocates so strongly with tradition, spirit, character, and wishes.
examples: In keeping with tradition, the outgoing chair gave the closing toast.
The addition is in keeping with the character of the block.
In keeping with the family's wishes, the service was private.
His decision was entirely in keeping with everything he had said publicly.
The raise is in keeping with what neighboring districts have offered.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈlaɪn wɪθ/ · weak /wəθ/ · also /wɪð/ before a vowel
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative headed by what (in line with what the committee recommended) — never a finite clause and never a gerund
entries.pattern: [clause] in line with [noun phrase] / In line with [noun phrase], [clause] / bring/come/fall in line with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Weaker than in accordance with, which implies obligation, and more quantitative than in keeping with, which is about spirit: earnings come in in line with expectations, but a memorial service is in keeping with someone's wishes. Keep the frozen phrase apart from the literal in line with the doorframe, meaning physically aligned, which uses the same three words. Its listing among the complex prepositions generally is at in line with.
entries.meaning: Reports that something matched a forecast, a policy, or a standard. It is the standard verb-free way for analysts and reporters to say "as predicted," and bring into line with is its transitive twin.
examples: Third-quarter results came in in line with analysts' forecasts.
Wage growth is now roughly in line with inflation.
In line with company policy, expenses over fifty dollars need a receipt.
The new rules bring the state in line with federal standards.
The proposal is broadly in line with what the committee recommended.

entries.ipa: /ɪn səˈpɔrt əv/ · weak /ɪn səˈpɔrt ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in support of raising the minimum wage) — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [clause] in support of [noun phrase] / In support of [noun phrase], [clause] / [document] in support of [motion] / evidence in support of [proposition]
entries.contrast: The exact mirror of in opposition to, and the two form the standard caption pair in American motion practice. Against in favor of, which states approval, in support of names something you are actively backing with an act, a document, or evidence: you are in favor of a bill, but you march in support of it. Against on behalf of, no authorization is implied.
entries.meaning: Names what an act, a document, or a body of evidence is backing. Unlike in favor of, which reports an opinion, this phrase attaches to something that was actually done. 1. Backing a proposal, a cause, or a person. 2. Offered as evidence for. 3. Providing assistance to an operation — military and logistical.
examples: Two hundred people rallied in support of the striking nurses.
She testified in support of the bill at Thursday's hearing.
In support of the application, the college submitted four letters.
There is very little data in support of that claim.
The affidavit was filed in support of the motion to compel.
Two cutters were dispatched in support of the search.
Guard units deployed in support of the county's flood response.

entries.ipa: /ɑn bɪˈhæf əv/ · weak /ɑn bɪˈhæf ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun — never a finite clause, never a gerund
entries.pattern: [clause] on behalf of [noun phrase] / On behalf of [noun phrase], [clause] / on [possessive] behalf — the possessive frame
entries.contrast: Against for, this specifies representation rather than mere benefit: a lawyer files on behalf of a client, but you buy a gift for a friend. Against in the name of, which invokes an authority, on behalf of names a principal. Against in support of and in defense of, which require no authorization, this one implies that you were asked. Its listing among the complex prepositions generally is at on behalf of.
variants: in behalf of was traditionally distinguished in American usage — on behalf of = "as the agent of," in behalf of = "for the benefit of" — but the distinction has collapsed and on behalf of now covers both. The reflexive is on my own behalf, never on behalf of myself. British usage is identical.
entries.meaning: Names the person or body an actor is representing. It is the standard opening of formal remarks and the standard signature line of counsel and agents, and its core claim is agency: somebody else's interest is being carried. 1. As the authorized agent or representative of. 2. Speaking for a group ceremonially or courteously. 3. For the benefit of — the older in behalf of sense, now absorbed into this one.
examples: The attorney filed the motion on behalf of her client.
The union bargains on behalf of eleven thousand members.
He signed the lease on behalf of the corporation, not personally.
On behalf of the entire staff, thank you for twenty years.
He accepted the award on behalf of his late father.
Neighbors organized on behalf of a family that lost everything in the fire.
She has lobbied on behalf of rural hospitals for a decade.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ðə ˈsaɪd əv/ · weak /ɑn ðə ˈsaɪd ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; in the err on the side of frame, an abstract noun naming a quality (caution, generosity, disclosure) — never a finite clause, never a gerund
entries.pattern: be on the side of [noun phrase] / come down on the side of [noun phrase] / err on the side of [quality] / on [possessive] side — the short frame
entries.contrast: Sense 1 declares an alliance and answers the question whose side are you on?. Sense 2, err on the side of, is a fixed idiom meaning "when in doubt, take too much of this rather than too little," and its complement is always a virtue, never a person. Against in favor of, sense 1 is about loyalty rather than about a position on a question; against in support of, it names a camp rather than an act.
variants: on X's side (history is on our side, the wind was on their side) is the ordinary short form. The literal spatial on the side of the hill is an ordinary of-phrase, not this preposition.
entries.meaning: Names the camp you belong to. Sense 1 is about loyalty in a dispute; sense 2 is a frozen idiom for deliberate overcorrection, and it takes a virtue rather than a party as its object. 1. Allied with; favoring in a dispute. 2. Err on the side of — deliberately overshooting a virtue.
examples: The building inspector was plainly on the side of the developer.
The court came down on the side of the tenants.
Time is on the side of whoever can afford to wait longest.
He liked to say he was on the side of the angels, which nobody believed.
When in doubt, err on the side of caution.
The policy tells reporters to err on the side of disclosure.
She erred on the side of generosity in every estimate she ever made.

entries.ipa: /proʊ/
entries.type: simple (marginal — from the Latin preposition; in American English overwhelmingly a prefix)
entries.register: informal as a free-standing preposition and more current in British English than American; the prefixed form is neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase only, usually bare (pro union, pro the merger) — never a clause, never a gerund. Distinguish the noun pro, meaning "a professional" or "an argument in favor" (the pros and cons), and the adjective (Is she pro or anti?), neither of which takes an object.
entries.pattern: be pro [noun phrase] / pro- [noun] as a prefix — the American norm / pro and con
entries.contrast: The mirror of anti. Neither is fully naturalized as a free preposition in American English, where in favor of and against do the work. The frozen pair pro and con — from Latin pro et contra — has become a noun idiom (the pros and cons) rather than a prepositional one.
variants: American style hyphenates the prefix before a capital or wherever the closed form would be misread (pro-American, pro-labor). The Latin phrases pro bono, pro rata, pro forma, and pro tem carry their own Latin objects and are not this preposition in ordinary English use.
entries.meaning: Declares the speaker on the same side as something. It is the shortest word in English for taking a position, which is exactly why it thrives as a prefix and struggles as a preposition.
examples: Nobody in that district is pro new taxes, whatever the polling says. (informal)
She's pro the merger but wants the timeline slowed down. (informal, British-flavored)
Pro-labor candidates swept the county races. (prefix — the normal American form)
The mayor is pro development in a way her predecessor never was.
We spent an hour on the pros and cons and settled nothing. (noun, not a preposition)
